text.p: On overnight commodity markets, copper prices fell on the London Metal Exchange after a lower than expected fall in stocks.

Gold bullion prices fell slightly as U.S. bond and stock markets rallied on the market's expectation that the Congress would still be controlled by fiscally frugal Republicans after today's election. News of a successful heart operation for Russian President Boris Yeltsin also did not help.
Wheat prices fell to new contract lows in Chicago on news of a good U.S. crop.
Oil prices were mixed on light volumes.

METALS - Copper prices turned lower during Tuesday afternoon LME trading, depressed by disappointed liquidation, and the market ended an undramatic session lower. Traders said the main catalyst for the trend was a smaller than expected warehouse stock fall of 2,525 tonnes. Although inventories are at fresh six-year lows, and there were no deliveries into Singapore the market is unconvinced. The selling in the afternoon put prices back below $1,970, and left chartists favouring the downside if there are no surprises in Wednesday's November option declarations. There is also the perception that the run of stock

drawdowns could be coming to an end soon, with metal expected to accumulate in Singapore that was shipped from Europe. Additionally, deliveries in Northern European warehouses may well be Chinese metal, which suggest that recent liftings by China may not be for consumption. Last three months business was at $1,961 a tonne, a $11 loss from Monday's kerb. Elsewhere in the base metals complex, movements largely mirrored copper, traders noted. However, aluminium proved resilient to the downturn in copper, as the market capitalised on early short-covering, as well as some protective buying ahead of Wednesday's options declarations which was designed to keep

downside puts out of play. The market was also aided by the 3,425-tonne drop in stocks, and final kerb trade was at $1,432, a $7.50 gain from Monday. Nickel's earlier rally was aborted in mid-afternoon, with prices drifting back in line with copper. The 720-tonne stock increase was also inhibitive, and by the end of the kerb the market was back at $7,150, down $10 from Monday. COMEX copper ended lower after a dull session, the market failing to gain momentum following a less-than-expected dip in LME stocks on Tuesday. December COMEX settled 1.40 cents weaker at 92.05 cents per pound, traded 93.50 to 91.60 cents. .

GOLD - New York precious metals ended mixed Tuesday, with light volumes light for the second day in a row, as the complex continued to consolidate after seeing multi-month lows last week. COMEX December gold ended unchanged at $379.60 an ounce, after trading in a $379.40-380.50 range on light estimated total volume of 18,000 lots. In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $378.50/379.00, compared to the London Tuesday afternoon fix at $379.25 and the New York close Monday at $378.60/379.00. Precious metals had discounted a win by President Clinton in the U.S. election Tuesday, and apparently successful heart surgery on Russian president Yeltsin overnight Monday reduced the risk

of political instability, reducing the incentive for investors to buy gold, traders said. A fresh fall in U.S. bond yields Tuesday to six month lows, after U.S. September house completions fell 5.8 pct, also meant there was no inflationary threat, and little need for gold as an inflation hedge, analysts said.

OIL - NYMEX crude and gasoline were off their session highs on Tuesday afternoon as expectations of a bearish distillate stock build in weekly inventory data weakened heating oil, traders said. December crude was up two cents at $22.81 a barrel

after rising to $23.09. In London IPE Brent crude futures ended lower, wiping out mild gains earlier in the session as traders anticipated further pressure on heating oil markets in the U.S. and Europe. Dealers said expectations of a further recovery in U.S. heating oil stocks on the release later on Tuesday of American Petroleum Inventory statistics undermined crude prices toward the close of the session.

CHICAGO - CBOT wheat futures closed sharply lower and new contract lows were set in all but the nearby December contract. An impressive rating for the 1997 U.S. winter wheat crop, building supplies of wheat worldwide, and falling prices all combined to drive the market lower, traders said. "It feels like total liquidation in here. First off the conditions were negative (bearish), Argentina is offering wheat at $124.00 (per tonne) and the EC is trying to get rid of wheat," said Skip Searcy, wheat trading specialist for Chicago-based trade house FIMAT Futures. USDA Monday said 75 pct of the U.S. winter wheat crop was in good to excellent shape as of Sunday, up from 56 pct

in that category a year ago. USDA also said 93 pct of the U.S. crop had been seeded as of Sunday, a hefty seedings level. The new contract low for March wheat is $3.63-1/2 per bushel, down from the previous low of $3.65-1/2 set Friday. Fund selling led the way down with Rosenthal Collins and Dean Witter Reynolds each a featured seller of two million bushels of December, the traders said. Wheat closed five to 11 cents per bushel lower, with December down 11 at $3.68-3/4.
